analyses.title: J-CRe3: A Japanese Conversation Dataset for Real-world Reference Resolution
analyses.research_question: How can real-world Japanese conversational reference resolution be studied with a multimodal dataset that links linguistic references, including omitted arguments, to concrete objects and regions observed in egocentric video?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct J-CRe3 from Japanese task-oriented conversations accompanied by egocentric video and audio, then annotate utterances, textual reference relations, object bounding boxes, persistent object-instance identities, and text-to-object links. Object tracks are initialized with Detic and StrongSORT and manually corrected, while textual annotations cover predicate-argument structures, bridging references, coreference, and zero references. They evaluate separate baselines for textual reference resolution and visual phrase grounding, including a Japanese-adapted MDETR model fine-tuned with external and J-CRe3 data.

key_findings.finding: J-CRe3 provides jointly aligned dialogue, video, textual-reference annotations, object boxes, persistent object-instance identifiers, and cross-modal reference links, including indirect and omitted references.
The annotation scheme can ground deictic expressions to spatial regions rather than requiring every reference target to be a discrete object.
Zero references are substantially more frequent than explicitly direct text-to-object references in the released annotations, making omitted arguments a central part of the benchmark.
The textual reference-resolution baseline reaches approximately 0.8 F-score and is reported as comparable to performance on established Japanese reference-resolution corpora.
Visual phrase grounding remains difficult: the strongest reported fine-tuned configuration reaches Recall@1 of 0.410 on J-CRe3, while pretrained-only configurations perform poorly.
Persistent object instance IDs maintain identity across video frames and therefore provide temporal object continuity, although they do not model lineage across revised document versions.

limitations: The dataset is relatively small because multimodal collection and annotation are expensive, and the authors state that it is insufficient for training the full task independently without external data.
The interaction domain is centered on a master and a domestic-assistant robot, so generalization to outdoor, multi-party, or multi-robot settings is not established.
The experimental pipeline resolves textual references and text-to-object references separately rather than with a single joint model.
The phrase-grounding experiment simplifies temporal grounding by considering frames in a restricted interval associated with each utterance.
Persistent identity is defined within a video sequence, not across revisions of a workbook, page, or other versioned artifact.
The dataset does not provide document-hierarchy provenance such as workbook-sheet-cell or document-page-region lineage.
raw_claims: J-CRe3 contains 93 recorded dialogues and 2,131 utterances aligned with egocentric video.
The video collection totals about 11,024 seconds and includes more than eleven thousand annotated frames.
Object annotations include class labels and instance identifiers that are kept consistent while an object is tracked through the video.
The dataset contains 79,694 bounding boxes associated with 1,741 object instances.
The annotation inventory covers 166 unique object classes.
Textual relations include predicate-argument structures, bridging references, and coreference.
The corpus contains 7,177 zero-reference annotations, substantially more than the explicitly direct reference annotations.
Text-to-object annotation can connect language either to object instances or to annotated spatial regions.
The best reported fine-tuned phrase-grounding configuration obtains Recall@1 of 0.410, Recall@5 of 0.494, and Recall@10 of 0.504.
The authors make the dataset and associated model resources publicly available.

analyses.title: Ferret-UI: Grounded Mobile UI Understanding with Multimodal LLMs
analyses.research_question: Can a multimodal large language model be adapted to high-resolution mobile user interfaces so that it both understands UI semantics and precisely grounds referring expressions to screen regions?
analyses.methodology: Ferret-UI extends Ferret with mobile-UI training data and an any-resolution processing strategy that represents a complete screen together with aspect-ratio-dependent subimages. Training combines elementary tasks such as OCR, icon recognition, widget classification, listing, referring, and grounding with more complex screen-description, conversation, interaction, and function-inference tasks. Android data are derived from RICO and iPhone data from AMP, with UI detector and OCR outputs used to construct annotations and GPT-4 used to generate advanced instruction data. The models are evaluated on 14 UI tasks against Ferret, task-specific baselines, and GPT-4V.

key_findings.finding: Specialized UI instruction tuning transforms the general Ferret model into a substantially stronger model for both referring and grounding of mobile-screen elements.

Ferret-UI outperforms GPT-4V on the paper's elementary UI categories, including several referring and grounding evaluations, while GPT-4V scores higher on the advanced conversational categories evaluated by a GPT-4 judge.
The any-resolution architecture improves several high-resolution UI results, most notably the reported iPhone advanced-task aggregate, but its benefit is not uniform across platforms.
In manually checked grounded conversations, Ferret-UI's predicted bounding boxes achieve 91.7% accuracy versus 93.4% for GPT-4V when GPT-4V is allowed to choose from predefined candidate boxes.

Adding elementary referring and grounding supervision improves performance on advanced UI-understanding tasks, indicating that explicit low-level grounding supervision benefits higher-level reasoning.

The quality and coverage of the upstream UI detector constitute a major bottleneck because visual properties or elements absent from detector-generated annotations cannot be learned reliably from that supervision.

limitations: The training annotation pipeline depends heavily on an upstream UI detector, so missed or poorly segmented elements propagate into the model's supervision.
Advanced instruction data are primarily generated from iPhone screens, and the any-resolution model shows weaker cross-platform behavior on some Android advanced evaluations.
The advanced-task evaluation uses GPT-4 as a judge, which may favor detailed generative responses and makes scores less directly interpretable than exact grounding metrics.
GPT-4V is evaluated on reduced subsets for some tasks because of inference cost, limiting the strength of direct comparisons.
Several advanced evaluation sets are small relative to the diversity of real mobile interfaces.
Training annotations combine automated detection, OCR, heuristic grouping, and synthetic GPT-generated text, so annotation errors can enter through multiple stages.
The model grounds elements within individual screen images but does not track the identity or lineage of an element across application versions or revised screens.
The representation has no native workbook-sheet-cell or document-version hierarchy.
raw_claims: Ferret-UI represents a high-resolution mobile screen using the global image together with two aspect-ratio-dependent subimages in its any-resolution variant.
Its referring interface can accept points, boxes, or free-form regions and can return grounded regions as outputs.
The elementary training curriculum includes OCR, icon recognition, widget classification, element listing, and several find-and-ground tasks.
The final training mixture contains about 250,000 examples spanning elementary and advanced UI tasks.
Android training images are drawn from a RICO-derived collection, while iPhone examples use AMP data.
Ferret-UI-base and Ferret-UI-anyres greatly outperform the unadapted Ferret model on the elementary UI benchmark categories.
On manually inspected grounded conversations, Ferret-UI obtains 91.7% bounding-box accuracy.
Adding elementary-task data improves advanced-task results compared with training only on advanced data.
The paper identifies detection quality as a bottleneck because undetected interface properties are missing from generated supervision.
The Ferret-UI release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and associated data resources.

analyses.title: Detecting Changes in XML Documents
analyses.research_question: How can two versions of a large XML document be compared efficiently to recover node correspondence and a compact edit description that includes subtree moves as well as insertions, deletions, and updates?
analyses.methodology: The paper develops an XML-tree differencing algorithm, BULD, that first establishes node correspondences and then constructs a delta between the old and new documents. It exploits XML ID attributes when available, computes signatures and weights for subtrees, matches large identical subtrees, and propagates matches bottom-up and lazily downward to find additional correspondences. The approach is evaluated with synthetically modified XML documents and a smaller collection of real web XML examples, measuring execution cost and the size or quality of generated deltas.

key_findings.finding: The algorithm explicitly models node correspondence between two document versions and can represent subtree moves in addition to insertions, deletions, and value updates.
XML ID attributes and subtree signatures provide strong anchors for preserving identity across versions, after which hierarchical propagation expands matches to related ancestors and descendants.

The implementation uses linear memory and exhibits approximately linear running-time behavior in the reported experiments, contrasting with earlier approaches characterized by the authors as quadratic.
On synthetically edited documents, the produced deltas are reported to remain reasonably close in size to the known edit scripts used to generate the modified versions.
On a small real-web sample, the XML-aware deltas have sizes comparable to conventional textual diff output while also encoding structural tree operations such as moves.
The method deliberately trades guaranteed global optimality for efficiency because optimal tree matching under the desired edit model is computationally difficult.

limitations: The heuristic matching algorithm does not guarantee a globally minimal or otherwise uniquely optimal delta.
Much of the empirical quality analysis uses synthetic mutations, whose distribution may not reproduce real editing behavior.
Only a small amount of real web XML data is presented because of space constraints.

The authors state that a fair comprehensive comparison with competing XML-diff systems would require substantially more experimentation because implementations, parsers, languages, and change distributions differ.
Delta byte size is only one possible quality criterion; the most useful correspondence can depend on downstream application semantics.
The method operates on XML tree structure and textual/attribute values rather than visual or multimodal document evidence.

There is no workbook-aware model of sheets, formulas, merged cells, row/column moves, or visual page regions, so applying it to revised spreadsheet provenance would require an additional domain-specific structural model.
raw_claims: The system compares two XML trees by identifying which nodes in the new tree correspond to nodes in the old tree.
Its delta language can express insertion, deletion, update, and movement of subtrees.
XML ID attributes are used as high-confidence correspondence anchors when the same identifiers occur in both versions.
The algorithm hashes subtree content so that identical subtrees can be recognized efficiently.
Large unchanged subtrees are matched before additional correspondences are propagated through the hierarchy.
The authors call the matching strategy Bottom-Up, Lazy-Down propagation.
The stated memory complexity is linear in document size.
Reported running cost grows almost linearly in the performance experiments.
Synthetic experiments apply controlled insertion, deletion, update, and move operations before attempting to recover a delta.
The authors note that producing an optimal change description is computationally hard and therefore use heuristic matching.
The real-document experiment is limited in scale and is not presented as a comprehensive benchmark against every XML differencing system.

analyses.title: Multi-Page Document Visual Question Answering using Self-Attention Scoring Mechanism
analyses.research_question: Can an OCR-free visual question-answering system select the page containing answer evidence from a long multi-page document using a lightweight self-attention scoring module while retaining competitive answer accuracy?
analyses.methodology: The system uses a Pix2Struct-based single-page DocVQA model and adds a self-attention scoring module that predicts how well each question-page pair matches. During scorer training, the underlying document model is frozen and each positive question-page example is paired with a randomly selected negative page, with the scorer trained using a smoothed regression target. At inference time every page is scored independently, the highest-scoring page is selected, and the existing encoder-decoder generates the answer from that page. Evaluation uses MP-DocVQA in its original form and an extended setting containing complete documents with hundreds of pages.

key_findings.finding: The proposed scorer achieves 81.55% page-selection accuracy on the original MP-DocVQA test set while remaining OCR-free.
The system reaches ANLS 0.6199 on the original test set, essentially matching the strongest reported competing multi-page result while using a smaller OCR-free architecture.
Selecting the first output vector from the self-attention scorer performs slightly better than the alternative aggregation strategies evaluated in the ablation study.
When evaluation expands from truncated documents to complete documents of up to 793 pages, test page-selection accuracy falls from 81.55% to 60.45% and ANLS falls from 0.6199 to 0.5394.

Some questions remain answerable even when the model selects a page different from the annotated evidence page; this occurs more often in the extended-document setting and reveals ambiguity in single-positive-page ground truth.
The approach provides explicit page-level provenance through its selected page, but it does not localize the supporting region, line, table cell, or element within that page.

limitations: The method assumes a single highest-scoring evidence page even though the authors' error analysis shows that multiple pages can sometimes support the same answer.
Inference processes every page separately, so total computation grows roughly linearly with document length even though per-page memory requirements stay bounded.
Page-selection accuracy degrades substantially when complete long documents replace the original truncated documents.
Correctly selecting a page does not guarantee a correct answer because the decoder can still fail to localize or reason over the relevant content within the page.
Ground-truth answers for the test set are not publicly available, so detailed error analysis is concentrated on the validation split while final test metrics rely on the evaluation server.
Negative training pages are randomly sampled rather than explicitly chosen as hard semantic or visual distractors.
The provenance granularity stops at the page level; it does not identify precise regions, table cells, or hierarchical document elements.
The method compares pages within one document instance and does not establish lineage between corresponding elements across document revisions.
raw_claims: The model is OCR-free and uses Pix2Struct as its visual document backbone.
Each question is rendered visually and concatenated with a document page before encoding.
A separate self-attention module scores whether each page matches the question.
Scorer training uses an annotated positive page and a randomly chosen negative page for each question.
At inference time the model scores all pages and sends the top-ranked page to the answer generator.
The proposed model obtains 81.55% page-prediction accuracy and 0.6199 ANLS on the original MP-DocVQA test set.
The extended test documents average 38.5 pages and include documents as long as 793 pages.
On the extended test set, page-prediction accuracy is 60.45% and ANLS is 0.5394.
On extended validation data, 6.88% of examples with a page-prediction mismatch nevertheless achieve a perfect answer-similarity score.
The paper provides public implementation code and uses the publicly available MP-DocVQA benchmark.

analyses.title: GRAVL-BERT: Graphical Visual-Linguistic Representations for Multimodal Coreference Resolution
analyses.research_question: Can multimodal coreference resolution in situated dialogue be improved by jointly encoding dialogue, candidate-object appearance, scene-graph spatial relationships, object metadata, conversational recency, and local environmental context?
analyses.methodology: GRAVL-BERT extends VL-BERT with a graph-convolutional representation of objects and their spatial relationships in a scene. Its inputs combine dialogue text, object metadata, reference-distance features, full-scene and candidate-region visual features, neighboring-object information, generated environmental captions, segment information, and positional signals. The model is trained for binary candidate-object classification on SIMMC 2.0, with dialogue-domain pretraining and negative downsampling, and predicts referred objects by thresholding candidate scores. Component ablations and error-category analyses measure the contribution of graph, recency, neighboring, and caption features.

key_findings.finding: GRAVL-BERT reaches approximately 0.78 F1 on SIMMC 2.0 and is reported as the strongest system among the compared challenge submissions.
Dialogue-domain pretraining alone markedly improves VL-BERT over the vanilla configuration, raising the reported development F1 from roughly 0.47 to roughly 0.68.
Adding graph-convolutional scene relationships raises development F1 further, showing that explicit spatial structure contributes useful grounding information.
Reference distance produces one of the largest incremental gains in the ablation sequence, supporting the usefulness of conversational recency for resolving referring expressions.
Neighbor features and generated environmental captions provide additional smaller improvements after graph and reference-distance features are included.

The paper's error analysis reports large reductions across spatial, dialogue-history, metadata, pure-visual, and non-target-object error categories relative to the dialogue-pretrained VL-BERT baseline.
The model grounds dialogue references to candidate scene objects but does not establish persistent object identity across revised versions of a document or interface.

limitations: Evaluation is limited to SIMMC 2.0's simulated fashion and furniture shopping environments, so behavior on natural documents, workbooks, emails, or production user interfaces is not established.

Dialogue context is restricted to three preceding turns because of transformer input-length constraints and an assumption that recent context is most relevant, limiting long-range reference resolution.
Environmental captions are generated by an additional vision-language pipeline and heuristically incorporated, creating another potential source of error.
The approach assumes a provided candidate-object inventory and scene relationships rather than evaluating end-to-end detection and relation extraction from unconstrained real images.
Each candidate object is scored as a binary decision with a fixed threshold, so performance depends on candidate generation and calibration.
The model resolves object coreference within a scene/dialogue context rather than lineage across artifact revisions.
It does not represent document-specific hierarchical coordinates such as version-page-region, workbook-sheet-row-column-cell, or attachment-version identifiers.
raw_claims: GRAVL-BERT combines visual-linguistic transformer representations with a graph representation of spatial relationships among scene objects.
The model uses SIMMC 2.0, a dataset of roughly eleven thousand task-oriented dialogues situated in virtual fashion and furniture environments.
Its graph encodes spatial relations such as left, right, above, below, and containment among candidate objects.
Reference distance represents how many dialogue turns have elapsed since the candidate object was most recently mentioned by the system.
Training uses dialogue-domain masked-language-model pretraining before multimodal coreference fine-tuning.
The vanilla VL-BERT baseline has development F1 around 0.47, while dialogue pretraining raises it to about 0.68.
Adding the graph component raises F1 to about 0.72, and adding reference distance raises it to about 0.77.
Neighboring-object features and generated captions provide further smaller gains, producing development F1 of about 0.783.
The reported test F1 is approximately 0.78 and the paper reports first place among the compared SIMMC 2.0 challenge systems.
The implementation is publicly released and the repository provides instructions for obtaining the SIMMC 2.0 data.
